questions.question: What does the Gen Z blame the previous generations (Boomers, Gen X, Millennials) for? / [CO1]

  • personal freedom. His violent rejection of the machines symbolizes his desire to reclaim

questions.question: Recount the key events of E. M. Forster’s "The Machine Stops". How do Vashti’s journey, Kuno’s room, and his confession highlight the dependence on the Machine? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Vashti, in E.M. Forster’s “The Machine Stops”, lives in total dependence on the Machine
  • — no human contact, air, light, and even ideas — her son Kuno insists that she visit him in
  • person, rejecting the Machine's mediated version of connection. Her journey exposes how
  • deeply "advanced" humanity has come to fear direct experience, as she reacts with horror to
  • sunlight, smell, and human touch. Unlike other rooms, Kuno's room symbolises resistance.
  • He questions the Machine's authority and longs for freedom. His room becomes a place
  • where independent thought survives, contrasting with the Machine's blind worship and
  • foreshadowing its destructive power. Kuno confesses to Vashti that he escaped to the Earth's
  • surface and discovered that the outside world is still habitable. In the end, V ashti and Kuno
  • are reunited as the Machine collapses, recognising that humanity's blind faith in technology
  • has led to its downfall. An(CO2)

questions.question: How does Ray Bradbury use exaggeration to critique society’s obsession with communication devices in "The Murderer"? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Ray Bradbury exaggerates the sheer saturation of communication technology in “The
  • Murderer” — offices piped with clashing soundtracks, a house that talks in every room, and a
  • bus full of commuters narrating their location to spouses — satirising how "convenience" has
  • metastasised into constant noise. Brock's reactions are levelled up to comic gestures (bite a
  • wrist radio in half, shoot a television six times, and spoon ice cream into a car radio
  • transmitter, turning ordinary appliance)-hatred into absurd, dramatic "murders" that expose
  • the disproportionate grip these devices hold over daily life. Through ‘anthropomorphism’- the
  • front door that "shrills," the stove that "screams," — Bradbury depicts machines as living
  • tyrants, making Brock's violence feel like self-defence rather than vandalism, which sharpens
  • the critique of how technology has usurped human agency. The image of the psychiatrist
  • absorbed into a barrage of ringing phones— after diagnosing Brock as "disoriented" —
  • delivers Bradbury's sharpest exaggeration and irony: society is so completely saturated by
  • devices that even the man meant to cure obsession is himself trapped by it, showing the
  • addiction to be systemic rather than individual. An(CO2)

  • with trivial things like drinking coffee- spreads the hold to meal planning, wardrobe- a
  • "phone tree" is designed recruiting users to enforce compliance on others-creates
  • conviniences- Abelique, the App deduces Linnea's suppressed interest in art from closet
  • photos- deduces Keith's managerial status from permission- authority becomes personal and
  • powerful. Abelique refuses to help Keith exploit it for workplace productivity-University
  • research reframes it as happiness experiment, not corporate control- but later, users become
  • reliant on imposed structure, App is exploited by spammers, algorithmic trust is questioned-
  • Linnea's invitation to a stranger to paint,shows the shifting authority to individual- Kritzer
  • suggets that algorithmic authority turns dangerous when it makes itself uncecessary.
